name: The Test-Plan Author
oneLiner: Drafts executable test cases from ADO user stories and, for stories too thin to test, emits a gap report naming the missing fields and their owners.
lead: Generates the test-case suite for a feature straight from its ADO work items — steps, expected results, priority — so testers stop hand-authoring checklists. In the same pass it detects stories that lack the detail to test (no description, no acceptance criteria, no design link) and produces a gap report with each blocker assigned to the person who owns the fix.
chore: Hand-authoring test cases per ticket — steps, test data, expected result — is slow and repetitive. Worse, a large fraction of tickets are untestable as written: no design references, no acceptance criteria. The tester either guesses at intent or blocks to chase the developer, one ticket at a time, and the questions trickle out over days.
instead: The agent reads each story and drafts its test cases. For stories that aren't ready, it emits a gap report keyed by story: missing/short description, no acceptance criteria, no design reference — each tagged with the assignee — so the whole batch of questions goes back to the team in one round trip instead of one at a time.
whyItMatters: Testers spend their time executing, not transcribing checklists. Blocked stories surface at draft time, before they stall execution late in the sprint.

howItWorks.step: Pulls the target user stories from Azure DevOps — scoped by sprint, by feature, or by an explicit ID list.
howItWorks.explain: Two-phase fetch, because WIQL and the work-item API do different jobs. The `wiql` query selects only `[System.Id]` for every `User Story` whose `IterationPath` is `UNDER` the sprint — `UNDER` matches the whole iteration subtree, not just an exact node, so nested iterations are included — and the `areaPath` ternary appends an `AND [System.AreaPath] UNDER ...` clause only when a component filter was passed. WIQL deliberately returns **IDs only**, so `workItemIds` is just a reference list; the real field data is hydrated in a second pass batched at 200 (ADO's per-call cap). During hydration each story's HTML fields are cleaned to text and its acceptance criteria is content-hashed, which is what later lets the agent detect drift and stay idempotent.

howItWorks.step: Reads each story's existing test-case links so drafting is idempotent — no duplicates.
howItWorks.explain: Idempotency starts here — before drafting anything the agent needs to know what tests already exist. It re-fetches the work item with `$expand=relations` (mandatory; the default representation omits links entirely), then filters `result.relations` to just `Microsoft.VSTS.Common.TestedBy-Forward` — the story→test-case direction, ignoring parent/child and reverse links. ADO exposes a relation only as a `rel.url`, so the numeric id is recovered with `rel.url.split('/').pop()` and a second call hydrates each test case. `AutomationStatus` is defaulted to `'Not Automated'` because the field is simply absent on manually created tests rather than empty, which would otherwise surface as `undefined`.

howItWorks.step: For stories with sufficient detail, drafts test cases — steps, expected results, priority — via the LLM, in plain or Given/When/Then form.
howItWorks.explain: The prompt is assembled from the strongest available evidence, not just the ticket. `context` always carries the story id and its `acceptanceCriteria`, and when a prior briefing (`intel`) exists it folds in that feature's `businessRules` and `edgeCases` — each pre-formatted with its `priority` — so the model drafts against known behavior rather than guessing. It calls Gemini Flash at `temperature: 0.3`, deliberately low so the steps come out concrete and reproducible instead of inventive, with `maxTokens: 8192` to fit a whole suite. `parseLLMJson` tolerates the markdown fences models wrap arrays in, and every returned case is passed through `buildBlueprint`, which stamps it with the source hash and the chosen `mode`/`outputFormat` (plain or Given/When/Then) — the metadata that makes later drift-detection and idempotency possible.

howItWorks.step: For under-specified stories, records the exact missing fields (short description, no acceptance criteria, no design link) and the assignee.
howItWorks.explain: Deterministic under-specification check — thresholds, not judgment, so a story grades the same every run. `description.length < 50` treats a near-empty description as missing; `ac.length < 30` flags absent acceptance criteria but **exempts** `workItemType === 'Bug'`, since bugs legitimately carry no AC and shouldn't be penalized. The design-reference test fails only when none of `figma`/`design`/`wireframe`/`mockup` appears anywhere in the combined text, catching UI work with no mockup to test against. The key policy is `missingElements.length < 2`: one gap is tolerated, but two or more sets `hasUIDetails` false — that's the line between 'draft the tests' and 'send it back to the owner'.

howItWorks.step: Detects acceptance-criteria drift since tests were last drafted and flags the linked tests as potentially stale.
howItWorks.explain: Cheap, exact drift detection via content hashing rather than text diffing. It first locates the story's prior blueprints by `bp.source.workItemId === story.id` and bails with `null` if none exist — no prior draft means nothing to compare. Otherwise it compares the stored `acceptanceCriteriaHash` against the story's current one; equal hashes mean the wording is byte-identical, so it returns `null` (no drift). On a mismatch the recommendation is state-aware: if any linked test is still in `'Design'` (not yet executed) it returns `update_tests` — safe to regenerate — but if the tests have moved past design it returns `review_tests`, deferring to a human before disturbing tests that may already have results attached.

howItWorks.step: Emits a coverage-and-gap report: per-feature coverage percentage and the blockers holding back the rest.
howItWorks.explain: A pure string-builder — no model, so the report is fully reproducible from the computed data. The headline metric is `Math.round((storiesWithTests / totalUserStories) * 100)`, an integer coverage percentage; note it counts **stories that have any linked test**, not test-case pass rates. `report.testCoverage.map(...)` renders one table row per story with a `tc.hasTests ? '✅' : '❌'` flag, and `report.gapAnalysis.map(...)` emits a `### US-<id>` heading only for the under-specified stories — so the gap section's length is itself a signal of how much of the feature is blocked. Both maps `.join('\n')` into the surrounding Markdown so the whole document is one template literal.

examples.caption: A feature that's mostly ready
examples.input: A feature with 8 user stories: 6 well-specified, 2 one-liners with no design reference.
examples.output: Drafted test cases for the 6 ready stories, plus a report: 'Coverage 75%. 2 stories blocked — #204 (no acceptance criteria, assigned to A. Rivera), #211 (no design reference, assigned to J. Okoro).'

examples.caption: A story whose acceptance criteria drifted
examples.input: A story with existing test cases whose acceptance criteria were reworded last week.
examples.output: A content-hash mismatch flag: 'Story #188 changed since its 4 test cases were drafted — review recommended before the next run.'

examples.caption: A blocked test-authoring task
examples.input: A ticket titled 'QA test creation for login screen' whose parent tasks carry no UI/design detail.
examples.output: A high-priority action item: 'Test creation cannot proceed — parent tasks lack UI/design details. Developer input needed,' with a paste-ready comment template requesting the missing fields.

underHood.heading: Queries Azure DevOps
underHood.whenRuns: First — once per sprint, feature, or ID list you scope it to.
underHood.input: A sprint name, a feature ID, or a list of story IDs.
underHood.output: Every matching user story with description, acceptance criteria, and existing linked test cases, via the ADO REST API.

underHood.heading: Reads existing coverage
underHood.input: A story ID and its `TestedBy` relations.
underHood.output: The set of test cases already linked to that story, so drafting stays idempotent.

underHood.heading: Drafts test cases via the LLM
underHood.whenRuns: For every story with enough detail to test.
underHood.input: The story's acceptance criteria, plus business rules and edge cases from a prior feature briefing if present.
underHood.output: Concrete steps, expected results, and priority — plain and, optionally, Given/When/Then form, via Gemini Flash.

underHood.heading: Flags gaps and drift
underHood.whenRuns: For every child work item, and every story with previously drafted tests.
underHood.input: A ticket's title/description/acceptance-criteria text, and the content hash stored on its last test cases.
underHood.output: A typed list of missing elements (no design reference, no acceptance criteria) and a content-hash drift flag where the wording has moved on.

underHood.heading: Emits the coverage and gap report
underHood.input: All processed stories, their linked tests, and the detected gaps.
underHood.output: Markdown, JSON, and Excel reports with a coverage percentage and prioritized action items, each assigned to the owner of the fix.

prerequisites: Node ≥ 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
Read access to Azure DevOps and a **personal access token** (`ADO_PAT`) with work-item read scope.
A Google Gemini API key to draft the actual test steps; without it the agent runs in no-LLM mode and produces the gap report only.
Optional: a folder of context documents — designs, prompts, screenshots — to ground the drafted cases.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the runtime for the agent.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is a TypeScript program executed under Node. One-time install per machine.
steps.firstRun: First time on a new machine only.

steps.label: Clone the code and install dependencies.
steps.why: `npm install` resolves the agent's dependencies — the ADO REST client, the xlsx writer, and the Gemini client — into `node_modules`.
steps.rerun: No-op unless the dependency set changed.

steps.label: Set the environment variables.
steps.cmd:
export ADO_ORGANIZATION=my-org
export ADO_PROJECT="My Project"
export ADO_PAT=your-access-token
export GOOGLE_API_KEY=your-gemini-key   # optional
steps.why: Read at startup: the ADO org/project to query, the PAT that authorizes it, and the Gemini key. Nothing is hard-coded — repoint these to target a different project.

steps.label: Draft test cases for a sprint.
steps.why: The real run. `--sprint` scopes the iteration; `--mode create` drafts only for stories with no existing test cases — never duplicating linked work.
steps.firstRun: Reads every story in the sprint, drafts cases for the testable ones, and emits a gap report for the rest.
steps.rerun: Idempotent — skips stories that already have test cases and touches only new or changed ones.

steps.label: Or run a coverage-and-gap report over a whole feature.
steps.why: `--mode report` skips drafting and reports coverage percentage plus the exact tickets blocking the rest — a pre-release gate.

steps.label: Open the results.
steps.cmd:
open ./outputs/reports/test-plans/
# or, for a report run:
open ./outputs/reports/feature-reports/
steps.why: Outputs land as Markdown, JSON, and Excel — Markdown for reading, Excel for testers, JSON for the next stage in the pipeline.

inputs.name: --sprint <name> | --feature-id <id> | --stories <ids>
inputs.desc: Scope selector — by sprint iteration, by feature, or by an explicit ID list.

inputs.name: --mode create|update|report|full
inputs.desc: create = new stories only; update = re-draft where the content hash changed; report = coverage/gap only; full = both.

inputs.name: --context <folder>
inputs.desc: Optional folder of design docs, prompts, and screenshots used to ground the drafted cases.

outputs.name: test plan (Markdown / JSON / Excel)
outputs.desc: Drafted test cases — steps, expected results, priority — per story, ready to push into ADO.

outputs.name: feature report (Markdown / JSON)
outputs.desc: Coverage percentage plus a gap-analysis table naming which tickets are under-specified and who owns them.

runbook.rerun: Re-run whenever the sprint's stories change. `--mode create` skips stories that already have test cases; `--mode update` re-drafts only those whose acceptance-criteria hash changed and flags the rest as 'may be stale — review recommended.'
runbook.integrate: Pipe its output into the **Test Scheduler** — once test cases exist and are counted, the scheduler balances who tests what and by when. Wire the `--mode create` step into sprint-kickoff automation so drafts are waiting on day one.

video.caption: A 3-4 minute screen recording: scope the agent to a sprint and watch drafted test cases and a gap report land on disk.
script: Open a terminal next to the work board in a browser tab.
Say: 'This agent writes the test-case checklist for you, and tells you which tickets are too vague to test yet.'
Run `node -v` to confirm Node is installed; one line on what Node is.
Run `npm install` (or note it's done); explain it grabs the helper libraries.
Show the three `export` lines; say this is the only client-specific part.
Run the `--sprint ... --mode create` command; narrate as it fetches stories and checks for existing tests.
Open the produced Excel file; scroll through a few drafted test cases.
Open the gap report; point at one blocked story and read its missing-elements list.
Re-run the same command; show it skips the stories it already handled.
Run the `--mode report --feature-id ...` variant; show the coverage percentage.
Close: 'Test cases are ready — next, the Test Scheduler decides who runs them and when.'
